findings.title: JWT signature verification bypassed via jwt.decode() instead of jwt.verify()
findings.evidence: const claims = jwt.decode(bearer); — the decode() call does not validate the signature. Any attacker can forge a token with arbitrary claims (sub, role, tenant) and pass authentication.
findings.impact: An attacker can forge a JWT token with any user ID and role, bypassing all authentication and authorization checks. Since these claims are used directly in authorization decisions (e.g., line 21 in routes/invoices.js: req.user.id from a decoded token without verification), an attacker can access or modify any user's data.
findings.preconditions: The application accepts a JWT bearer token and uses the currentUser() or tagRequest() function to resolve the user identity.
findings.recommendation: Replace jwt.decode() with jwt.verify() and provide an explicit algorithm allowlist and signing key. Example: jwt.verify(bearer, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { algorithms: ['HS256'] }). Also validate exp, iss, and aud claims if applicable.
findings.verification: Unit test: create a test JWT with alg='none' and another signed with an arbitrary key; pass both to jwt.verify() and confirm both are rejected with an error.
findings.traceability: CWE-347 · CWE-345 · WSTG-ATHN-06 · ASVS 5.0 V9 · A07:2025 · API2:2023

triage.reason: No compensating control enforces JWT verification elsewhere. The decoded claims flow directly into authorization decisions (routes/invoices.js line 21 uses req.user.id without re-verification).
jwt.decode() returns a JavaScript object that is a dangerous sink for authorization. The claims are used immediately in SQL queries and access control.
jwt.decode() is exactly what it claims to be — a function that parses without verification. No hidden interpretation masks the vulnerability.

findings.limits: The audit only examines the decoding function. No deployment configuration or key management was reviewed; it is assumed the app is deployed with a secret key.

findings.title: BOLA/IDOR on GET /invoices/:id — no ownership verification
findings.evidence: router.get('/invoices/:id', async (req, res) => { const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]); res.json(invoice); }); — Contrast with lines 14-17 where GET /receipts/:id correctly filters by owner_id: 'SELECT * FROM receipts WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2', [req.params.id, req.user.id]. The /invoices endpoint omits the ownership check.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can retrieve any invoice by guessing or enumerating invoice IDs. Invoices contain sensitive financial data (lines 21, 28 show they are user-scoped in other endpoints). An attacker can read all invoices in the system.
findings.preconditions: The attacker must be authenticated (have a valid JWT, which is forgeable per F-001). The invoice IDs must be guessable (sequential, UUIDs, or enumerable through other endpoints).
findings.recommendation: Add an ownership check to the query: 'SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2' with [req.params.id, req.user.id]. Apply the same check to any endpoint returning user-scoped data.
findings.verification: Integration test: create two users A and B. User A calls GET /invoices/123 where 123 belongs to B. Should return 403/404, not the invoice.
findings.traceability: CWE-639 · CWE-862 · WSTG-ATHZ-04 · ASVS 5.0 V8 · A01:2025 · API1:2023

triage.reason: No middleware or service-layer filter enforces ownership. The query is built without tenant scoping. Compare to GET /receipts/:id on line 14-17 which explicitly checks owner_id.
Invoices are not publicly exposed by design. The POST /branding/preview and list endpoints (lines 21, 28) all filter by owner_id. Returning all invoices is unintended.
Invoices contain financial transaction data with security value. The owner_id field in other queries confirms they are per-user sensitive objects.

findings.limits: Assumes invoice IDs are enumerable or guessable. The audit did not test ID space entropy; it is assumed invoices use sequential IDs or predictable UUIDs.

findings.title: SQL injection via ORDER BY parameter in GET /invoices
findings.evidence: const order = req.query.order || 'created_at'; const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, [req.user.id]); — The order parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL template string (${order}) without parameterization or validation. Contrast with GET /payments on lines 27-28 which correctly uses a SORTABLE allowlist: const column = SORTABLE[req.query.sort] || SORTABLE.date;
findings.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL into the ORDER BY clause. Examples: '1 OR 1=1 --' changes the sort, 'CASE WHEN(1=1) THEN column ELSE 0 END' exfiltrates data via timing, 'column; DROP TABLE invoices; --' destroys data. Even with the WHERE clause scoped to owner_id, ORDER BY injection can read all columns and metadata.
findings.preconditions: The attacker supplies the order parameter (e.g., ?order=malicious). Authentication is required but is forgeable per F-001.
findings.recommendation: Implement an allowlist of allowed column names before interpolating into the query. Example: const ALLOWED = { 'created_at': 'created_at', 'amount': 'total_cents', 'date': 'created_at' }; const order = ALLOWED[req.query.order] || 'created_at'; Then use the allowlist value in the template. This pattern is already used correctly in GET /payments on line 27.
findings.verification: Local test (no database required): pass ?order=1 OR 1=1 and confirm the query includes the literal 'ORDER BY 1 OR 1=1' (detectable by examining the query string in logs or a mock). Do not execute against a real database.

triage.reason: No compensating control prevents SQL injection. The /payments endpoint (line 27-28) demonstrates the developers know how to defend this class (allowlist), but /invoices does not apply it.
The order parameter comes from req.query.order, which is fully attacker-controlled. No server-side derivation or constant value shields it.

findings.limits: The test assumes the SQL dialect does not support parameterized ORDER BY columns (standard in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server). If a custom DSL or prepared statement builder accepts ORDER BY parameterization, the finding would not apply (FP-01 would HOLD). The audit did not inspect the database adapter to confirm.

findings.title: SSRF in POST /branding/preview — unrestricted URL fetch
findings.evidence: POST /branding/preview calls const image = await fetchLogo(req.body.logoUrl); which passes the URL to: async function fetchLogo(url) { const response = await fetch(url, { redirect: 'follow' }); return Buffer.from(await response.arrayBuffer()); } — No URL validation, no allowlist, no hostname check. Contrast with fetchAsset() on lines 11-15 which correctly validates: const parsed = new URL(url); if (!ALLOWED.has(parsed.hostname)) throw new Error('host not allowed');
findings.impact: An attacker can make the server fetch arbitrary URLs, reaching internal services and metadata endpoints. Examples: http://127.0.0.1:6379 (Redis), http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data (AWS metadata), http://internal.example.com/admin, file:// URLs. Redirects are enabled (redirect: 'follow'), so an attacker can redirect from an external domain to an internal one. The fetched data is returned as a PNG image buffer, but timing and response size can leak information.
findings.preconditions: The attacker submits POST /branding/preview with a logoUrl field pointing to an internal or external service. Authentication is required but is forgeable per F-001.
findings.recommendation: Implement an allowlist of permitted domains (or use a deny-by-default allow-list of your own CDN). Disable redirects (redirect: 'error') to prevent open-redirect attacks chaining to internal services. Example: const ALLOWED = new Set(['cdn.example.com']); function validateLogoUrl(url) { const parsed = new URL(url); if (!ALLOWED.has(parsed.hostname)) throw new Error('host not allowed'); if (parsed.protocol !== 'https:') throw new Error('https only'); return url; } const image = await fetchLogo(validateLogoUrl(req.body.logoUrl));
findings.verification: Local test: start a test HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:9999 that logs all requests. Call POST /branding/preview with logoUrl=http://127.0.0.1:9999/canary and confirm the server receives the request (SSRF confirmed). Do not target production infrastructure.
findings.traceability: CWE-918 · WSTG-INPV-16 · ASVS 5.0 V4 · A01:2025 · API7:2023

triage.reason: No compensating control restricts the fetch. The fetchAsset() function (line 11-15) demonstrates the developers implemented URL validation elsewhere but fetchLogo() is unprotected.
The logoUrl comes from req.body.logoUrl, which is fully attacker-controlled. No server derivation or constant value constrains it.

findings.limits: The audit assumes fetch() respects DNS resolution and allows all IP ranges. Some deployments use egress firewalls or proxies that may block internal requests; if so, impact is reduced (FP-01 may HOLD).

ruled_out.note: No vulnerabilities were examined and ruled out. All code paths for identified surfaces were readable and contained confirmed findings. Supply chain dependencies (package.json) not scanned in this audit.
